notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **Jeremiah 8**, drawn from the approved sites.

---

## Overview

Jeremiah 8 continues the temple sermon begun in chapter 7. No break exists between the chapters; the “at that time” of v. 1 refers to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans described at the end of chapter 7.[¹] The chapter moves from the desecration of graves (vv. 1–3) to Judah’s irrational refusal to repent (vv. 4–7), the false wisdom of the scribes (vv. 8–9), the judgment on corrupt leaders (vv. 10–13), the people’s panic and the invaders' approach (vv. 14–17), and finally Jeremiah’s lament (vv. 18–22). The twin themes are Judah’s stubborn rebellion and her inevitable doom.[²]

---

## Verses 1–3: The Desecrated Graves

**v. 1:** “At that time” ties directly to the judgment of Jeremiah 7:32–34. The enemy (whether Chaldeans or later the Romans, as Gill allows) would open the tombs of kings, princes, priests, prophets, and ordinary citizens.[³] Ellicott notes the motives could be either wanton ferocity of barbarian conquerors bent on mutilating the dead, or greed for buried treasures—as when Hyrcanus later broke open David’s sepulchre.[⁴] Guzik calls this “a final indignity” and “the highest expression of hatred and contempt in ancient culture.”[⁵] Constable adds that ancients believed the spirits of unburied people had no rest in the netherworld.[⁶] The fivefold repetition of “the bones” has the emphasis “as of the toll of a funeral bell.”[⁷]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 2:** The bones would be spread before the very heavenly bodies they had worshipped—sun, moon, and stars. Ellicott observes that five verbs (“loved…served…followed…consulted…worshiped”) trace a progression from inward impulse to full ritual idolatry.[⁸] Craigie (cited by Constable) notes the grim irony: “as if in fulfillment of the desires of the dead, their bones are laid out…exposed to the very astral ‘powers’ whom once the dead had worshiped”—but these deities are now “uncaring, complacently shining in the heavens, unconcerned about human fate.”[⁹] Unburied bones would become “like dung”—human remains serving as fertiliser, an ultimate dishonour.[¹⁰]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 3:** The surviving exiles would prefer death over life. Gill explains the misery of the scattered remnant would be so severe that death would seem a welcome relief.[¹¹] Constable connects this to the curses of Leviticus 26:36–39 and Deuteronomy 28:65–67, and notes Revelation 9:6 echoes the same sentiment.[¹²]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

---

## Verses 4–7: Judah’s Stubborn Refusal to Return

**v. 4:** The Lord asks two commonsense questions. Ellicott translates, “Shall men fall and not arise? Shall one turn away and not return?”[¹³] When people fall, they naturally get up. When someone takes a wrong path, he retraces his steps. In its spiritual aspect, Ellicott says, the words “assert the possibility of repentance in all but every case, however desperate it may seem,” and he links it to Paul’s question in Romans 11:11: “Have they stumbled that they should fall?”[¹⁴] Constable similarly says the point is that “it was normal for people to repent after sinning.”[¹⁵]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 5:** Yet Judah had done the unnatural thing. The Hebrew root *shub* (“turn, repent”) occurs repeatedly in vv. 4–5, highlighting the irony.[¹⁶] Ellicott reads “a perpetual turning” (backsliding)—“here, so far, there was no retracing the evil path which they had chosen.”[¹⁷] Guzik says the Lord “expressed amazement that Judah would not return to Him”; G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) says, “If men fall it is naturally expected that they will return. In the case of Jerusalem this had not been so, their backsliding had been perpetual. There was no sign of repentance.”[¹⁸] They “cling to deceit” and “refuse to return.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 6:** God (or the prophet) “listened and heard” but found no one speaking what is right. No one repents saying, “What have I done?” Gill notes that the impenitent man does not even ask this question; a true answer would reveal deeds “deserving of the wrath of God, and eternal death.”[¹⁹] Everyone “pursued his own course like a horse charging into battle.” The Hebrew word for “rushes” is used of a torrent flooding (Isaiah 8:8), suggesting frantic impetuosity into evil.[²⁰] Constable remarks they “were refusing to acknowledge their sin…headed for trouble, like a horse rushing headlong into battle.”[²¹]

Spurgeon preached a sermon titled *“What Have I Done?”* on this verse. The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary lists it as a topic: “INTERROGATING OUR CONDUCT.”[²²]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 7:** Even migratory birds—the stork, turtledove, swift (or crane), and thrush (or swallow)—know their appointed seasons and obey their God-given instinct. But “My people do not know the requirements [judgment / ordinance] of the LORD.” Ellicott notes that the Hebrew name for stork, *chasideh* (literally “the pious bird”), is suggestive—it cares for its young, yet Israel does not.[²³] Spurgeon preached an entire sermon, *“Migratory Birds,”* making four points: birds know when to come and go, where to go, the way to go, and they actually go. Humans are worse than “bird-brained” creatures.[²⁴] Guzik echoes this: “They were worse off than birds with small brains.”[²⁵]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-8.html (Spurgeon referenced)

## Verses 8–9: The False Wisdom of the Scribes

**v. 8:** The people boasted, “We are wise, and the Law of the LORD is with us.” But their scribes, using their pens (the iron stylus for engraving), had turned God’s truth into a lie through sophistry and misleading casuistry.[²⁶] Ellicott sees Jeremiah here as “foreshadowing the prophet of Nazareth” (cf. Matthew 5:20–48; 23:2–26) in his protest against traditional, misleading scribal teaching.[²⁷] Constable says the scribes “kept official records, copied important documents, and taught the people the Law,” but had perverted it so that the people could claim obedience while disobeying.[²⁸] Gill adds that the scribes made “false glosses and interpretations,” by which “the word of God was made of none effect.”[²⁹]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 9:** The “wise men” (perhaps distinct from scribes—students of the sapiential books like Proverbs)[³⁰] would be put to shame, dismayed, and trapped. “Since they have rejected the word of the LORD, what wisdom do they really have?” Guzik notes: “Though they claimed to have both wisdom and Biblical truth, they had neither. In rejecting God’s word, they rejected wisdom.” He quotes Morgan: “the manner of such wisdom is…‘earthly, sensual, devilish’ (James 3:15).”[³¹]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm

## Verses 10–13: Judgment on Corrupt Leaders

**v. 10:** Verses 10–12 largely repeat Jeremiah 6:12–15. Guzik says the repetition “was not accidental. It was done on purpose, because Judah needed to hear this message, and delivering it one time was simply not enough.”[³²] Because from least to greatest all are greedy for gain, and from prophet to priest all deal falsely, God would give their wives to other men and their fields to new owners (the invaders).[³³]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 11:** The false prophets and priests “healed the wound of the daughter of My people slightly” (or superficially), saying “Peace, peace” when there was no peace. Spurgeon preached *“Healed or Deluded? Which?”* on this text, warning how easy it is to be “deluded into a slight healing” rather than seeking true healing from the Lord.[³⁴] Constable calls this providing “panaceas” while all was far from well.[³⁵]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/healed-or-deluded-which (referenced in search results)

**v. 12:** The leaders felt no shame for their abominations—“they do not even know how to blush.” Therefore they would “fall among the fallen” in the coming punishment. Constable cites Thompson: “Could men reach a stage of apostasy where they would never repent? Yes they could, and Judah had reached that point [cf. Hebrews 6:4–6].”[³⁶]

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**v. 13:** God would “take away their harvest.” Ellicott notes the Hebrew literally reads “Gathering, I will sweep away,” the two verbs being nearly identical in sound—an emphatic reduplication.[³⁷] There would be “no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither.” Constable sees this as figurative: God went looking for a harvest of righteousness but found only withered leaves (cf. Isaiah 5:2; Matthew 21:18–19; Luke 13:6–9; John 15:2). So He would remove their former blessings.[³⁸] Gill notes grapes and figs were the chief fruits and stand for the whole harvest.[³⁹]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

## Verses 14–17: Panic and Approaching Invaders

**v. 14:** The prophet dramatises the people’s cry: “Why are we just sitting here? …let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there.” Ellicott says they flee “without hope…into the silence as of death, for to that silence Jehovah himself has brought them.”[⁴⁰] The “poisoned water” (water of gall) is a bitter, deadly potion—Ellicott suggests possibly belladonna, colocynth, or poppy; it signifies both bitterness and poison.[⁴¹] The people at last acknowledge: “because we have sinned against the LORD.” Yet Gill notes “it does not appear that they had true repentance…sometimes confession of sin is made without either of these.”[⁴²]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**v. 15:** The people “hoped for peace…for a time of healing, but there was only terror.” This is the bitter fruit of believing the false prophets’ “Peace, peace!” of v. 11.[⁴³] Ellicott renders “a time of healing, and behold alarm”—the false hope collapses.[⁴⁴]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm

**v. 16:** The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan—Israel’s northernmost city, so the invasion from the north is first detected there.[⁴⁵] “The whole land quakes” at the sound. The enemy comes “to devour the land and everything in it, the city and all who dwell in it.” Ellicott mentions a patristic interpretation that this indicates the coming of Antichrist from the tribe of Dan, but calls it “one of the eccentricities of exegesis.”[⁴⁶]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**v. 17:** God says He will send “snakes…vipers that cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.” The imagery shifts suddenly to serpents, likely recalling the fiery serpents of Numbers 21:6 or the connection of Dan with serpents in Genesis 49:17.[⁴⁷] Ellicott identifies the “cockatrice” (KJV) as probably the *cerastes* or horned viper, noting that serpent-charming was well known in Egypt and India from earliest times. The point: these serpents “cannot be charmed”—the enemy is implacable, waging pitiless war (cf. Psalm 58:4–5, the “deaf adder”).[⁴⁸] Guzik applies it: the false prophets had convinced the people they could “maneuver around the coming judgment,” but “they would find, to their great sorrow, that God had sent them serpents which cannot be charmed.”[⁴⁹]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

---

## Verses 18–22: Jeremiah’s Lament

**v. 18:** “My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me.” The prophet speaks in his own voice. Ellicott renders it as a cry: “Ah, my comfort against sorrow! …my heart is sick within me” (cf. Isaiah 1:5).[⁵⁰] Constable says the prospect of the invasion “overwhelmed Jeremiah with sorrow. It made him weak, and he could not get over his anguish.”[⁵¹] Guzik quotes Spurgeon: “A preacher whom God sends will often feel more care for the souls of men than men feel for themselves or their own salvation.”[⁵²]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**v. 19:** Jeremiah hears the cry of the exiles “from a land far away”: “Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?” This is asked “half in despair, and half in murmuring complaint,” says Ellicott.[⁵³] But God answers with His own question: “Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images, with their worthless foreign idols?” Guzik says: “The problem was not that God had abandoned the land of Israel; the problem was Israel had abandoned God.”[⁵⁴]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**v. 20:** “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.” This is one of the most famous verses in Jeremiah. Constable says it was “a popular proverb used in daily life when men encountered a hopeless situation.”[⁵⁵] Cundall (cited by Guzik) explains: “‘Harvest’ refers to the main cereal harvest, whilst ‘summer’ refers to the vintage harvest (grapes, etc.) in early autumn. If one failed, it was possible that the other would see the people through the winter, but if both failed, starvation confronted them.”[⁵⁶] Guzik adds: “The season had come when there should be abundance in the land, yet there was not.”

Spurgeon preached an entire sermon on this verse titled *“Harvest Past, Summer Ended, and Men Unsaved.”* He applied it evangelistically: seasons of spiritual opportunity come and go; to remain unsaved after many such seasons is a terrifying condition. Spurgeon wrote in *Morning and Evening*: “Not saved! Dear reader, is this your mournful plight? …Years have followed one another into eternity, and your last year will soon be here: youth has gone, manhood is going, and yet you are not saved.”[⁵⁷]

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/harvest-past-summer-ended-and-men-unsaved (referenced)
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/morneve/morneve.d1231pm.html (referenced)

**v. 21:** “For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed. I mourn; horror has gripped me.” Ellicott says Jeremiah “is crushed in that crushing of his people. His face is darkened, as one that mourns” (cf. Psalm 38:6; Joel 2:6).[⁵⁸] Guzik notes: “Jeremiah could mourn over the sufferings of his people because of his sympathy and love for them; yet his very message spoke doom to them” (quoting Thompson).[⁵⁹]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**v. 22:** “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?” Gilead (east of the Jordan) was famous for its healing balsam—a resinous gum from the storax tree (or possibly the *Pistaccia lentiscus*), exported even to Egypt for embalming (Genesis 37:25).[⁶⁰] The question is a parable: “Are there no means of healing, no healer to apply them, for the spiritual wounds of Israel? The prophets were her physicians, repentance and righteousness were her balm.”[⁶¹] Guzik notes the balm “might be compared to aloe vera.”[⁶²] Constable says no physician was on the horizon, even though Yahweh was Israel’s Great Physician (Exodus 15:26)—“the prophet marveled that Israel’s Great Physician had not provided healing for His people, but he knew that their affliction was judgment for their sins.”[⁶³] Gill explains the question shows “the stupidity, sluggishness, and indolence of the people, and how inexcusable they were.”[⁶⁴] This verse is the source of the traditional spiritual “There Is a Balm in Gilead.”[⁶⁵]

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

## Denominational Distinctives

Because Jeremiah 8 is a prophetic oracle of judgment, the traditional literal-historical reading is broadly consistent across Protestant traditions. Differences arise more in homiletical application than in exegesis:

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** The emphasis falls heavily on personal, individual repentance. Spurgeon’s sermons on v. 6 (“What have I done?”), v. 7 (“Migratory Birds”), v. 11 (“Healed or Deluded?”), and v. 20 (“Harvest Past…”) all press toward individual conversion. Spurgeon’s *Morning and Evening* on v. 20 bluntly asks the reader, “Will you ever be saved? …Are not the probabilities dead against your ever being saved?” This urgency of personal decision is characteristically Baptist. Gill’s exposition treats the chapter as a denunciation of Jewish impenitence but reads it as applying to all who reject God’s word.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-8.html
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/harvest-past-summer-ended-and-men-unsaved (referenced)
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/8.htm

**Reformed Baptist / Calvinistic (John Piper, Desiring God):** Piper does not have a verse-by-verse commentary on Jeremiah 8, but his broader handling of Jeremiah emphasises the sovereignty of God in judgment and restoration, the futility of idols, and that God Himself is the fountain of living waters—the ultimate good of the gospel (citing Jeremiah 2:12–13). This God-centred framework shapes Reformed readings of the judgment passages: the tragedy is not merely suffering but forsaking God Himself.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-died-to-bring-you-to-god

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word):** Guzik’s commentary stays close to the conservative evangelical reading, with strong application emphasis. He stresses the role of true versus false prophets, the danger of rejecting God’s word, and the compassion of the prophet. The distinct Pentecostal note is not in exegetical divergence but in the expectation that God’s word through His servants should produce active response.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-8/

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott’s treatment is historically and linguistically careful. He notes the rhetorical structure, the Hebrew wordplay, and connects the imagery to the wider biblical canon. His comment on v. 8 that Jeremiah “foreshadows the prophet of Nazareth” reflects an Anglican comfort with typological and Christological reading of the Old Testament.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/8.htm

**Lutheran, Methodist, Wesleyan/Holiness, Orthodox, Catholic:** I was unable, within the search and fetch limits, to retrieve specific Jeremiah 8 commentary from the approved Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), or Orthodox (oca.org) sites. No results were returned that offered verse-by-verse treatment of this chapter from those traditions' own teachers.

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Constable / NET Bible notes):** Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) provides archaeological and historical context: astral worship was popular under Manasseh (2 Kings 21:3; 23:4) and revived after Josiah’s reforms (Ezekiel 8:16); the practice of grave-robbing was common in the ancient Near East; the balm of Gilead was resin from the storax tree.[⁶⁶] Constable dates these prophecies to Jehoiakim’s early reign (shortly after 609 B.C.).[⁶⁷]

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-8.html

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Could not be retrieved within the allowed search and fetch limits on the specified sites. No results were found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for verse-by-verse Jeremiah 8 commentary.

**Debated Popular Modern Teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No results were found from the approved sites addressing Jeremiah 8 from these perspectives. The chapter’s theme of irrevocable judgment for unrepentant sin sits uneasily with prosperity and hyper-grace frameworks; the approved sites do not appear to host material making those connections.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

1. **Judgment fits the crime:** Bones are exposed to the very astral deities the people worshipped (vv. 1–2).
2. **Sin is irrational:** It defies nature—even migratory birds obey God-given instinct, but God’s people do not (vv. 4–7).
3. **False teachers are deadly:** Those who claim wisdom but reject God’s word, and who cry “Peace” when there is none, are agents of destruction (vv. 8–12).
4. **There is a point of no return:** Shameless, perpetual backsliding leads to judgment from which there is no charming the serpents (vv. 13–17).
5. **The prophet weeps:** Jeremiah models godly anguish over sin and its consequences. His closing question about the balm of Gilead—for which there is no answer in the chapter—hangs as a haunting, open wound (vv. 18–22).
